extracted.intended_audience: K-12 teachers and school leaders (literacy educators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for teaching, assessing, and implementing the Six Traits of Writing (ideas, organization, voice, word choice, sentence fluency, conventions) across K–12 classrooms, including lesson structure, feedback, and rubric-building. Emphasizes trait-based mini-lessons, conferences, kid-friendly rubrics, and schoolwide implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait of Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a single topic to convey a clear message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach knowledge-based topics, writing for a purpose, narrowing a topic, details/development/elaboration, supporting ideas with examples, and (for narratives) developing plot, characters, and setting. Treat many discrete standards/skills as 'raindrops' that fall under the Ideas umbrella and teach them explicitly over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait of Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Reveal ideas in a logical order, including a beginning, middle, and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach pre-writing and planning, grouping like ideas, hook and ending components, clear transitions, and sequential organization. Use genre-specific structures (persuasive: What & Why; how-to/informative: chronological steps; narrative: Who, What, & How).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait of Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase reader engagement with intentional writer feeling, attitude, and emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach writing to an audience, building a reader-writer connection, expressing the writer’s feelings about the topic, using voice with typographic choices (e.g., NO, !!!, yuck) intentionally, and shifting attitudes/perspective within a piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait of Word Choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the right word in the right place to convey just the right meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach specific nouns, descriptive adjectives tied to the five senses, action verbs, imagery (show, don’t tell), synonyms/varied word choice, and appropriate adverbs to sharpen meaning and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait of Sentence Fluency
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve the readability of a piece with complete thoughts and sentence variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach complete sentences, varied sentence beginnings, different sentence types (simple, compound, complex) and punctuation (.!?), varied sentence lengths, oral readability (read aloud), and use of figurative language to create flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait of Conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make writing more correct by following the rules of spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and grammar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach proper capitalization, paragraph indents, grammar and mechanics, punctuation usage (,;—’…”), readable spelling, and correct spacing/wrapping. Emphasize conventions appropriate to the developmental level (including pictorial/writing fundamentals for PK–1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation (6+1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional trait addressing presentation/visual appearance of the product (handwriting, typography, layout, graphics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation includes penmanship, legibility, margins, white space, and in digital work: typography, color, and graphics. The guide emphasizes that presentation is valued by readers but does not substitute for content quality, so it is treated separately from the six core traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce the Six Traits (rollout)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial rollout should intentionally introduce the six trait terms and language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set aside 1–2 mini-lessons per trait (6–12 days total) to establish a common vocabulary. Be consistent (use parallel mentor texts/approaches for each trait), be visual (use graphic icons and yearlong bulletin boards or digital equivalents), and embed the same icons/language schoolwide when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mini-lesson structure and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily mini-lessons should be short (10–15 minutes) and include four essential steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: STEP 1: Introduction—announce a small, focused target skill and identify its trait. STEP 2: Instruction—teacher models the skill with Think Alouds (I do). Think Aloud tips: announce the I do, avoid eye contact, speak in first person, and plan the Think Aloud. STEP 3: Interaction—We do work together (use Turn & Talk and Back to Me to engage students). STEP 4: Closure—You do: set the student response/practice activity. Keep lessons mini so students practice during writing time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think Aloud practice (teacher modeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Think Alouds in instruction to reveal expert thinking while modeling a skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the Think Aloud carefully (teachers must slow down automatic skills), speak in first person about decisions, avoid seeking student help during the I do, and use the Think Aloud to show when/where/how/why a skill is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression for teaching a single skill (Notice it / Name it / Try it / Apply it)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach one focused skill across multiple mini-lessons rather than introducing a new skill every day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule 3+ days per skill: Day 1 Notice & Name (study mentor/authentic text), Day 2 Try It (teacher models inserting the skill into draft), Day 3 Apply It (students use the skill while composing a first draft). Use this slow, repeated approach to support mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait-based feedback: conferencing types
rubrics_metrics.description: Use conferences for formative feedback: Product conferences and Process conferences serve different purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product conferences: 15–25 minutes, infrequent (3–4 times/year) focused on final draft strengths/areas to improve. Process conferences: brief, frequent (minutes), occur at any stage (topic selection, drafting, revision) and can be individual or small-group to reach more students more often.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait-based feedback: compliments and comments
rubrics_metrics.description: During conferences provide a specific trait compliment (strength) and a trait-labeled comment (area for improvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label each compliment/comment with its trait umbrella (e.g., 'Word Choice: awesome verbs; Sentence Fluency: vary sentence length'). Use a cheat sheet during conferences and provide targeted, concise feedback—conference is a conversation, not an edit session.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build kid-friendly Six-Traits rubrics collaboratively
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a rubric WITH students describing what each trait looks like at HIGH, MIDDLE, and LOW performance levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-construct descriptors for HIGH, MIDDLE, LOW; map them to Levels 1, 3, and 5 then add Levels 2 and 4 in between. Creating rubrics with students produces kid-friendly language, ownership, and clearer guidance for revision. Accompany student work with the rubric and highlight relevant criteria instead of writing repetitive comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principles for grading with Six-Traits rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: Three grading principles to follow when using the rubric to assign grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) NO ONE CAN FAIL ON THE RUBRIC: Level 1 should still be passing (e.g., D-), only missing submissions fail. 2) HONOR THOSE WHO GO BEYOND THE GOAL: include an exceeding/A+ level. 3) DON’T WEIGH TRAITS EQUALLY: vary trait weighting depending on the assignment (e.g., conventions may weigh less on first drafts; poetry may emphasize word choice and fluency). Communicate weights before students write.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting rubric scores to grades (calculator workflow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a rubric-calculator approach rather than naively summing levels as points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: 1) Identify which traits to score. 2) Determine the value for each trait. 3) Read the student’s piece. 4) Select each trait score. 5) Calculate earned grades/points/percentage. The guide warns: avoid simply adding up rubric levels as points and recommends using the Smekens Six-Traits Rubric Calculator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align traits to state/national standards and assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Six Traits map onto state and national writing standards and testing rubrics, though not always by the same labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study assessment criteria and ask which trait each skill impacts. The guide provides color-coded links mapping Common Core and multiple state standards to the six traits and notes that Ideas and Organization are often the 'trophy' traits emphasized on tests (SAT, ACT, Smarter Balanced, PARCC, state rubrics). Use these mappings to prioritize instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize teacher resources by trait
rubrics_metrics.description: Store lesson plans, mentor texts, anchor papers, and materials in trait-based folders to ease lesson planning and retrieval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create six digital folders or physical files—one per trait—or use labeled mini-lesson labels for hanging files. Housing materials by trait helps teachers quickly find resources tied to the specific skills they teach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make mini-lessons more engaging (use triggers and mentor text)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase engagement by pairing the target skill with a concrete trigger and authentic mentor texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a trigger that mirrors the function of the skill (e.g., Russian stacking dolls to teach narrowing a topic). Use authentic mentor texts (picture books, articles, student anchor papers) rather than contrived workbook examples to show the skill in real writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schoolwide implementation & professional development
rubrics_metrics.description: For schoolwide fidelity, provide ongoing professional learning and collaborative structures to support Six-Traits use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with building a shared understanding of traits across genres/levels; use book studies, on-site PD by Six-Traits experts, on-demand workshops, instructional rounds, PLC time to examine implementation, and instructional coaching. Implementation requires more than posters—it requires daily explicit teaching linked to trait language and repeated exposure across years.
